questions.question: Interpret how the number of comparisons in linear search and binary search changes as the dataset size increases. / [CO1] MAHATMA GANDHI UNIVERSITY, KOTTAYAM Discipline Specific Core Course (DSC) - MG3DSCCSC201 - DATA MGU-UGP (Honours)/MGU-BBA (Honours)/MGU-BCA (Honours) Special Examinations, July 2026 (for 2024 Admission Regular Examinations, October 2025)Third SEMESTER
questions.solution_html:
• Interpret how the number of comparisons in linear search and binary search changes
  • as the dataset size increases.
  • Answer:
  • As the dataset size increases, the number of comparisons required by linear search and
  • binary search changes differently. As the dataset size increases, the number of comparisons
  • required by linear search and binary search changes differently.
  • • Linear Search
  • o Checks each element one by one until the target is found.
  • o As the dataset grows, the number of comparisons increases linearly
  • (proportional to n).
  • o Worst-case time complexity: O(n).
  • • Binary Search
  • o Works only on a sorted dataset.
  • o Divides the search space into two halves after each comparison.
  • o As the dataset grows, the number of comparisons increases very slowly
  • (logarithmically).
  • o Worst-case time complexity: O(log₂ n).
  • For small datasets, both methods may perform similarly. However, as the dataset becomes
  • larger, binary search requires far fewer comparisons than linear search, making it much
  • more efficient for searching in sorted data.
  • Marking Scheme (5 Marks)
  • Explains linear search comparisons increase linearly 2
  • Explains binary search comparisons increase logarithmically (halving concept) 2
  • Correct comparison table/conclusion 1

questions.solution_html:
• Illustrate the step-by-step changes in a stack (array representation) when the
  • following operations are performed: push(10), push(20), pop() and push(30)
  • Answer:
  • A stack is a linear data structure that follows the LIFO (Last In First Out) principle. In an
  • array implementation, the variable TOP keeps track of the topmost element in the stack.
  • Initial Condition
  • • Stack Size = 5
  • • TOP = -1 (Stack is empty)
  • Operation 1: push(10)
  • Step
  • • Increment TOP by 1.
  • • Insert 10 at index 0.
  • Operation 2: push(20)
  • Step
  • • Increment TOP.
  • • Insert 20 at index 1.
  • Operation 3: pop()
  • Step
  • • Remove the element at TOP.
  • • Decrement TOP.
  • Operation 4: push(30)
  • Step
  • • Increment TOP.
  • • Insert 30.
  • Marking Scheme (5 Marks)
  • Definition of stack and LIFO principle 1
  • Correct illustration of push(10) and updated TOP 1
  • Correct illustration of push(20) and updated TOP 1
  • Correct illustration of pop() with deleted element and updated TOP 1

questions.question: Define circular queue and list its basic operations. / [CO2] [15x1 = 15]
questions.solution_html:
• Define Circular Queue and list its basic operations.
  • Answer
  • A Circular Queue is a queue in which the last position is connected back to the first position,
  • forming a circle. It follows the FIFO (First In First Out) principle and efficiently utilizes
  • memory by reusing empty spaces created after deletions.
  • Need for Circular Queue (2 Marks)
  • In a linear queue, after several dequeue operations, empty spaces at the beginning cannot be
  • reused.
  • A circular queue overcomes this problem by allowing the rear pointer to wrap around to the
  • beginning of the array.
  • Array Representation (2 Marks)
  • • Queue is stored in an array.
  • • Two pointers are maintained:
  • o Front → points to the first element.
  • o Rear → points to the last element.
  • Initially,
  • Front = Rear = -1
  • Basic Operations (6 Marks)
